title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Pierre had rarely seen his wife alone lately. Both in Petersburg and in Moscow their house was always full of guests. The night after the duel he didn't go to his bedroom but instead, as he often did, stayed in his father's room — that enormous room where Count Bezukhov had died.

He lay down on the sofa intending to fall asleep and forget everything that had happened, but he couldn't. Such a storm of feelings, thoughts, and memories suddenly overwhelmed him that he couldn't sleep or even stay in one place. He had to jump up and pace the room with rapid steps. One moment he seemed to see her in the early days of their marriage, with bare shoulders and a languid, passionate expression on her face, and then immediately he saw beside her Dolokhov's handsome, insolent, hard, and mocking face as it had been at the banquet — and then that same face, pale, trembling, and suffering, as it had looked when he staggered and sank into the snow.

"What has happened?" he asked himself. "I've killed her lover — yes, killed my wife's lover. Yes, that's what happened! And why? How did I come to do it?" — "Because you married her," answered an inner voice.

"But how was I to blame?" he asked. "For marrying her without loving her; for deceiving yourself and her." And he vividly recalled that moment after supper at Prince Vasili's when he had spoken those words he found so hard to say: "I love you." "It all comes from that! Even then I felt it," he thought. "I felt then that it wasn't right, that I had no right to do it. And so it has turned out."

He remembered his honeymoon and blushed at the memory. One recollection was particularly vivid, humiliating, and shameful — how one day, shortly after his marriage, he had come out of the bedroom into his study a little before noon in his silk dressing gown, and found his head steward there. The man bowed respectfully, glanced at his face and his dressing gown, and smiled slightly, as if expressing a tactful understanding of his master's happiness.

"But how often I was proud of her — proud of her majestic beauty and social skill," he thought. "I was proud of my house, where she entertained all of Petersburg, proud of her cool composure and beauty. So this is what I was proud of! Back then I thought I didn't understand her. How often, when thinking about her character, I told myself that I was the one at fault for not understanding her, for not understanding that constant poise and self-satisfaction and complete lack of interests or desires. And the whole secret lies in the terrible truth that she is a corrupt woman. Now I've said that terrible word to myself, everything has become clear."

"Anatole used to come to borrow money from her and would kiss her bare shoulders. She didn't give him the money but let herself be kissed. Her father once tried, as a joke, to make her jealous, and she replied with a calm smile that she wasn't stupid enough to be jealous. 'Let him do what he wants,' she used to say about me. One day I asked her if she had any signs of pregnancy. She laughed scornfully and said she wasn't fool enough to want children, and that she wasn't going to have any children by me."
Then he recalled the coarseness and bluntness of her thoughts and the vulgarity of her expressions, despite her aristocratic upbringing.
"'I'm not that stupid.... Just you try.... Get lost,' she used to say. Seeing how successful she was with young and old men and women, Pierre often couldn't understand why he didn't love her.
* "Get lost."

"Yes, I never loved her," he said to himself. "I knew she was a corrupt woman," he repeated, "but I didn't dare admit it to myself. And now Dolokhov is sitting in the snow with a forced smile, perhaps dying, while I face my remorse with some kind of forced bravado!"
Pierre was one of those people who, despite appearing to have what's called a weak character, don't seek a confidant when they're in trouble. He processed his suffering alone.

"It's all her fault," he told himself. "But what does that matter? Why did I tie myself to her? Why did I say 'I love you' to her — which was a lie, and worse than a lie? I'm guilty and must endure... what? A stain on my name? A lifelong misfortune? Oh, that's nonsense," he thought. "A stain on my name and honor — that's something separate from who I really am."
* I love you.

"Louis XVI was executed because they said he was dishonorable and a criminal," the thought came to Pierre. "And from their point of view, they were right — just as those were right who made him a saint and died as martyrs for his sake. Then Robespierre was beheaded for being a tyrant. Who is right and who is wrong? No one! But if you're alive — live. Tomorrow you'll die, just as I might have died an hour ago. And is it worth tormenting yourself when you have only a moment of life compared to eternity?"

But the moment he imagined himself calmed by such thoughts, she suddenly came into his mind as she had been in those moments when he'd most strongly expressed his fake love for her, and he felt the blood rush to his heart and had to get up again and move around and smash and tear at whatever came to hand. "Why did I tell her 'I love you'?" he kept repeating to himself. And after saying it for the tenth time, Moliere's words came to him: "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?" — and he began to laugh at himself.
* "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?"

During the night he called his valet and told him to pack for Petersburg. He couldn't imagine how he could face her now. He decided to leave the next day and write her a letter informing her of his intention to separate from her forever.
The next morning, when the valet came in with coffee, Pierre was lying asleep on the ottoman with an open book in his hand.
He woke up and looked around for a while with a startled expression, unable to grasp where he was.
"The countess asked me to inquire whether your excellency was at home," said the valet.

But before Pierre could decide what answer to send, the countess herself entered the room. She wore a white satin dressing gown embroidered with silver, her hair simply arranged — two thick braids wound twice around her lovely head like a crown. She was calm and majestic, except for an angry crease on her rather prominent marble forehead. With unshakable composure she didn't speak in front of the valet. She knew about the duel and had come to discuss it. She waited until the valet had set down the coffee things and left. Pierre looked at her timidly over his spectacles, like a hare that, surrounded by hounds, flattens its ears and crouches motionless before its enemies — he tried to go on reading. But realizing this was pointless and impossible, he glanced at her timidly again. She didn't sit down but stood looking at him with a contemptuous smile, waiting for the valet to leave.
"Well, what's this about? What have you been up to now, I'd like to know?" she asked sternly.
"Me? What have I...?" Pierre stammered.
"So you're a hero now, are you? Come on, what was this duel about? What is it supposed to prove? What? I'm asking you."
Pierre rolled over heavily on the ottoman and opened his mouth but couldn't reply.

"If you won't answer, I'll tell you myself..." Helene continued. "You believe everything people tell you. You were told" — Helene laughed — "that Dolokhov was my lover," she said with her characteristic blunt directness, tossing out the word as casually as any other, "and you believed it! Well, what have you proved? What does this duel prove? That you're a fool — but everybody already knew that. What's going to happen now? I'll be the laughingstock of all Moscow. Everyone will say that you, drunk and clueless about what you were doing, challenged a man you were jealous of for no reason." Helene's voice rose and she grew more and more agitated. "A man who is better than you in every way..."
"Hmm... hmm..." Pierre growled, frowning without looking at her and not moving a muscle.
"And how could you believe he was my lover? Why? Because I enjoy his company? If you were more intelligent and more pleasant, I'd prefer yours."
"Don't talk to me... please," Pierre muttered hoarsely.
"Why shouldn't I talk? I can say whatever I want, and I'll tell you plainly that very few wives with husbands like you would have avoided taking lovers — but I haven't done that," she said.

Pierre wanted to say something. He looked at her with a strange expression she didn't understand, then lay down again. He was in physical agony at that moment — there was a weight on his chest and he couldn't breathe. He knew he had to do something to end this suffering, but what he wanted to do was too terrible.
"We should separate," he muttered in a broken voice.
"Separate? Fine, but only if you give me a fortune," said Helene. "Separate! As if that's supposed to scare me!"
Pierre leaped up from the sofa and rushed staggering toward her.
"I'll kill you!" he shouted, and seizing the marble top of a table with a strength he'd never felt before, he took a step toward her, brandishing the heavy slab.

Helene's face became terrified. She shrieked and sprang aside. His father's nature showed itself in Pierre. He felt the thrill and ecstasy of rage. He hurled down the marble slab, shattering it, and lunging toward her with outstretched hands, he roared "Get out!" in such a terrible voice that the whole house heard it with horror. God knows what he would have done if Helene hadn't fled the room.
A week later Pierre gave his wife full control over all his estates in central Russia, which made up the greater part of his wealth, and left for Petersburg alone.
